evidence_quotes.quote: Since the late 19th century such commons serving farming households have been subsidized by the State. In this article, we develop a conviviality lens to analyze how water commons are being supported and regulated by public institutions.

The fieldwork for this article was conducted by the main author, who was first employed at the department for agriculture and forestry of the Canton (Landwirtschaft und Wald, LAWA) responsible for supporting rural water schemes (Feb. 2021 – June 2022) and then by the private engineering company planning the described project (since July 2022).

These insights were enriched by in-depth, semi structured interviews with six government officials (four current and two former), five scheme officials, three engineers, two local politicians and one contractor. In addition, the historical and the newspaper archive of the Canton was consulted.
Outsourcing of annually recurring tasks therefore either results in reduced time availability for planning activities and consultation processes, or in higher planning costs.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 8, Development of Infrastructural Options
evidence_quotes.quote: Without these subsidies, it would become too expensive for cooperative N to pursue the independent refurbishment of their own reservoirs and they would instead be forced to join the inter-connection option.

evidence_quotes.quote: Members of the steering committee later stated that while being aware of the decision power of the Canton, they were convinced that they could win, if they decided to challenge this decision in court. They explained though, that this would be expensive and time consuming and that it was not in their interest to engage in such a confrontation with the Canton.

country.comment: The study examines rural collective water supply schemes in the Canton of Lucerne (Luzern), Switzerland. Note: The retrieved full-text PDF is Hofstetter, Bolding, & Boelens (2023), 'Conviviality Under Pressure of Market-Modernist Expertocracy: The Case of Water Commons in Rural Switzerland', International Journal of the Commons 17(1):375-389 (DOI: 10.5334/ijc.1256), rather than the Water 15(21):3736 article listed on the blind-sheet header; all fields are extracted strictly from the provided PDF full text.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 2, Introduction

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative case study; no statistical point estimates, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported. Descriptive figures reported in the text include cantonal support staff declining from 14 (1973) to 3 (2008) before rising to 4 (2022), commercial engineering rates of 140-160 USD/hour against a 1.5 million USD annual cantonal budget, an estimated 8% cost difference for renovating Cooperative N's independent reservoirs, and Cooperative N's 14-to-4 general assembly vote to continue connection planning.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Outside built-up municipal zones in the Canton of Lucerne, rural citizens are legally self-responsible for water supply via user-run cooperatives historically supported by federal and cantonal agricultural subsidies (up to 30% cantonal plus matching federal share) and public engineering staff. New Public Management (NPM/WOV) legal reforms (1995 pilot; 2001 cantonal law) outsourced technical planning to commercial engineering consultants and reduced cantonal support staff from 14 employees (1973) to 3 (2008), increasing planning costs and shrinking consultation time. In the case study of interconnecting three rural cooperatives (S, K, and N) following the 2018/19 drought and a food-safety regulatory ultimatum on Cooperative N's reservoirs, cantonal officials and outsourced engineers pushed for scheme merger and professionalization, withholding federal subsidies and threatening indeterminate delays in cantonal subsidies for Cooperative N's independent reservoir renovation. Cooperative N blocked a full organizational merger—securing an umbrella fourth cooperative for the shared reservoir—and voted 14 to 4 to continue connection planning, illustrating how top-down expert planning and discretionary subsidy conditionality undermine autonomous, convivial rural water governance.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by qualitative study design (CASP). Rated 2 because the study directly observes and documents the administrative, planning, and subsidy-allocation mechanisms operating in real time through embedded participant observation inside both the cantonal authority (LAWA) and the private engineering firm, triangulated with 17 stakeholder interviews and cantonal/federal legal records.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 2, Introduction; PDF pp. 5-10, Project Phases and Case Study Sections

mechanism_flags.comment: Spatial zoning separates municipal urban water responsibility from rural self-supply outside built-up zones, while subsidy eligibility restricts support to agricultural households (ELIGIBILITY: zoning, service_area, property). Two-step municipal/cantonal subsidy applications, outsourced NPM engineering planning, commercial planning/pumping cost burdens, and threatened delays in subsidy disbursement shape project feasibility (BURDEN: planning, procedural_steps, fees, delay, bureaucratic_assistance). Cantonal officials exercise wide discretion to withhold federal subsidies to force interconnection, limit user co-design/participation, coordinate across municipal/insurance/cooperative bodies, while food-safety authorities enforce reservoir standards via ultimatums and cooperative leaders weigh but forgo costly judicial review (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT: discretion, participation, political_coordination, judicial_review).
